item.title: Trump says US has 'massive' munitions stockpile, vows 'treasonous' leakers being hunted down
item.description: Trump says the U.S. has a "massive" munitions stockpile and vows "treasonous" leakers will face long jail sentences after reports of depleted weapons.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump declared Thursday that the U.S. has a "massive" munitions stockpile and "treasonous" leakers are "being hunted down" after reports emerged claiming the U.S. Army has burned through nearly all of its stockpiles of two of its primary long-range precision weapons.

The Army has used "virtually all" of its inventories of Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) during the five-month conflict with Iran, Reuters reported Tuesday, citing people familiar with internal U.S. military data.

"The U.S. has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types. Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed. Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history," Trump wrote on Truth Social early Thursday.

"The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!" the president added.

ALARMING MISSILE REPORT DRAWS FORCEFUL RESPONSE FROM TRUMP AS IRAN WAR TESTS AMERICA’S ARSENAL

Trump’s message was reposted on X by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.

If accurate, the Reuters report underscores a longstanding Pentagon concern: America's most sophisticated precision weapons can be expended in months but often take years to replace.

Officials fear the drawdown could complicate the military's ability to respond to future crises involving adversaries such as China and Russia, according to the report.

WEAPONS STOCKPILE SHORTAGES IMPACTING MILITARY STRATEGY IN THE MIDEAST

Reuters also reported that the conflict significantly reduced inventories of Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors, along with Tomahawk cruise missiles, though the Pentagon has maintained the U.S. military retains the capabilities needed to carry out operations worldwide.

Exact U.S. weapons stockpile figures remain classified for national security reasons.

Some estimates show the U.S. has used more than half of its stockpiles of some weapons systems in the war with Iran. The Center for Strategic and International Studies found the U.S. has enough missiles to continue fighting in Iran under any plausible scenario, but the group says the true issue with the shrinking stockpiles is future wars.

"The depletion of munitions was a major topic and a major reason for the suspension of air attacks," Mark Cancian, a retired U.S. Marines colonel and senior advisor with the CSIS Defense and Security Department, told Fox News' Bret Baier. "Our inventories were getting way below what the war planners wanted. That might encourage China to do something."

CSIS notes many munition stockpiles are substantial but focused its analysis on seven key weapons that have been effective in Iran and would also be valuable in a possible Pacific conflict.

Trump said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital on Wednesday that, "We have far more munitions than anyone in the world, and far more than we need, despite the fact that an unprecedented amount was given away by Crooked Joe Biden and the Biden Administration to Ukraine and Europe at no cost, in one of many of their extremely dumb moves."

The Pentagon has also pushed back on the reporting.

"America’s military is the most powerful in the world and has everything it needs to execute at the time and place of the President’s choosing. We have executed multiple successful operations across combatant commands while ensuring the U.S. military possesses a deep arsenal of capabilities to protect our people and our interests," chief spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement.

Fox News' Bret Baier and Amy Munneke and Fox News Digital's Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

item.title: Sanders' answer when asked if he will endorse socialist Hong in Wisconsin sparks instant mockery: 'Says a lot'
item.description: Bernie Sanders says he won't endorse DSA member Francesca Hong's Wisconsin governor bid, sparking mockery given his support for other candidates.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., was asked if he would endorse Democratic Socialist of America (DSA) member Francesca Hong’s Wisconsin gubernatorial bid, and his response sparked immediate mockery on social media.

"I don’t think so," the Vermont socialist told "Pod Save America" host Jon Favreau when asked if he is going to endorse Hong’s campaign for governor. "I met Francesca a couple of years ago. I was in Wisconsin, and she seems very, very nice, but again this is a race I’m just not that familiar with."

Sanders added that "we have not gotten involved in many governors' races" other than recently in Maine, where he endorsed Democrat Troy Jackson, who ultimately replaced disgraced Senate candidate Graham Platner, a candidate Sanders endorsed.

Political commentators quickly chimed in on social media suggesting that Sanders not endorsing Hong shows the senator doesn’t think she can win, with many pointing to Sanders’ strident support of Platner despite all of his political baggage.

AFTER PLATNER IMPLOSION, MAINE DEMOCRATS RUSH TOWARD NEW SENATE NOMINEE DESPITE FRESH WARNING SIGNS

"Bernie says he’s not backing Francesca Hong because he’s focused on the Senate," Washington Free Beacon reporter Chuck Ross posted on X. "Yet he’s endorsed in mayoral races, House races, and Troy Jackson’s failed governor race in Maine. That’s how whacky Hong is".

"Says a lot," Politico reporter Will Steakin posted on X.

"Guy with the Nazi Tattoo ‘hey everyone makes mistakes’," conservative commentator Stephen L. Miller posted on X. "Crazy communist lady - ‘not my cup of tea sorry.’"

SOCIALIST FRONTRUNNER IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER 'CANCEL THANKSGIVING' POST EMERGES ONLINE

"This guy endorsed a guy with a natzi [sic] tat but thinks @FrancescaHongWi is not worth an endorsement……," Jerry Ponio, legislative director for Americans for Prosperity - Wisconsin, posted on X. "Yikes."

"Well, I guess even Bernie enjoys celebrating Thanksgiving at one of his three houses," an account ran by Hong’s likely general election opponent, Republican Tom Tiffany, posted on X.

Tiffany’s post references a controversial quote from Hong that went viral on social media where she suggested canceling Thanksgiving.

"Francesca Hong, who is a Socialist candidate for Governor of Wisconsin is too radical...even for Bernie Sanders," Turning Point Action Northeast Manager Brandon Maly posted on X.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Hong campaign and Sanders’ office for comment.

Critics have argued that Francesca Hong's politics are too far to the left for a swing state like Wisconsin, contending that her identification as a socialist and support for ambitious progressive policies could make her less competitive in a general election.

Hong’s social media account is littered with far-left pledges like abolishing the U.S. Senate and defunding the police.

Hong recently tried to walk back those positions in recent interviews ahead of Tuesday’s gubernatorial primary against Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, former Wisconsin Department of Administration secretary Joel Brennan, and Democratic state Sen. Kelda Roys.

Polls suggest Hong is likely to comfortably win that contest, which will advance her to a race against Tiffany, the likely Republican nominee, in November.

item.title: Miss North Carolina USA loses crown after organizer condemns 'racism, homophobia, transphobia'
item.description: Brittany Boltinhouse lost her Miss North Carolina USA crown weeks before the national pageant over conduct the organization says violated its standards.
item.content:encoded:
Miss North Carolina USA was stripped of her crown weeks before the Miss USA pageant after organizers cited an extended pattern of conduct violating the organization's standards.

Miss USA Chairman Thom Brodeur did not specify what conduct prompted the decision to take the crown away from Brittany Boltinhouse but said in a statement that the organization "does not tolerate racism, homophobia, transphobia nor language that strips any person of their dignity," adding the conduct occurred "over an extended period of time."

The decision ends Boltinhouse's reign just weeks after she won the state title and less than three weeks before she was scheduled to represent North Carolina at the 75th annual Miss USA pageant on Aug. 27.

SEN BERNIE MORENO CALLS FOR EX-SON-IN-LAW TO RESIGN FROM HOUSE, GET 'SERIOUS PSYCHOLOGICAL HELP'

Myla Hadley, the first runner-up in the state competition, will now represent North Carolina on the national stage "with our full confidence and our support," Brodeur said in a statement.

Brodeur said the decision was made in consultation with Boltinhouse, her state directors and the Miss USA organization. He added that while the organization has a "zero tolerance" standard for conduct, accountability "is not permission to strip someone of their humanity."

"There is a young woman at the center of this," Brodeur said. "She has been named, examined, and judged in public in a way that most of us would not survive, and she is still a human being with a family, a future, and a life ahead of her that is longer than this part of her journey."

"I have never believed that accountability requires cruelty, or that holding a line means enjoying the fall of the person who crossed it," he continued.

Brodeur said Boltinhouse plans to issue her own statement to speak to the matter "in her own voice." The chairman said he has reviewed her statement and described it as showing "ownership, accountability and apology."

"I believe people can change," Brodeur said. "Change is not a statement. It is a record. It is built over time, in the open, through conduct rather than apology alone."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Boltinhouse for comment.

WASHINGTON POST OPINION EDITOR TO EXIT PAPER AFTER JUST ONE YEAR, STAFF COMPLETELY 'BLINDSIDED'

State pageant organizer A Blaize Productions similarly announced the decision after what they described as a "thorough review of recently surfaced information" but did not elaborate on the nature of the allegations.

"We ask our pageant family, supporters, and the public to extend kindness and respect to both Brittany and Myla during this transition," the organization said in a statement. "Moments like these are never easy for anyone involved, and we remain committed to treating everyone with dignity while continuing our mission of empowering the next generation of women leaders."

Hadley acknowledged the abrupt transition in a social media post, saying she understands "the seriousness and level of prestige that this title carries."

"While this may seem like a two-week turnaround given the circumstances, I've been preparing to represent at Miss USA since I first competed with this organization," Hadley wrote. "I am ready to represent North Carolina."

item.title: NCAA ignored the warnings. Now It's fighting for survival in courtrooms across America over eligibility
item.description: The NCAA's decision to exclude the 2022 class from its five-year eligibility rule triggered a wave of lawsuits and court injunctions nationwide.
item.content:encoded:
The NCAA has spent the past few years pleading with Congress to help rein in the chaos engulfing college athletics, with a large chunk of the focus centered on the wave of lawsuits challenging student-athlete eligibility.

At this point, it feels like a daily occurrence. The organization tasked with enforcing its own rules is constantly reacting to another lawsuit filed in state or federal court by an athlete seeking an additional year of eligibility.

While NCAA officials continue lobbying lawmakers to pass the 'Protect College Sports Act'—which would provide the organization with greater antitrust legal protections against these challenges—they had the opportunity to avoid the chaos centered around the most recent flurry of lawsuits themselves.

When the NCAA adopted its new age-based eligibility model, giving athletes five years to play five seasons, it made one critical decision that is being argued in courtrooms across the country on a daily basis: it excluded the 2022 recruiting class from the new rule.

From that moment on, pure chaos has reigned down upon state courtrooms, while senators try to push the 'Protect College Sports Act' through congress.

Tennessee Coach Unloads On NCAA's 'Bulls–t', After Star Linebacker Suspended For Outdated Rule

Athletes who believed they were unfairly denied an extra season of competition began filing civil lawsuits across the country, arguing they should receive the same benefits as those covered under the new eligibility structure.

Had the NCAA implemented the five-and-five rule a year earlier—or simply grandfathered in the 2022 class—college athletics might not be facing its current legal mess that has lawyers fielding more phone calls than a 9-1-1 operator on a Saturday during the football season in a college town.

One of the bigger problems in the aftermath of some injunctions granted is that there are too many athletes and not enough roster spots. As college football teams open fall camp to prepare for the 2026 season, there are not just a plethora of open spots on the roster left for those who now have eligibility, or will gain eligibility.

INDIANA TAKES FULL ADVANTAGE OF NCAA COURTROOM CHAOS WITH STUNNING ROSTER MOVE AMID ELIGIBILITY FIGHT

In college basketball, teams were anticipating the potential for madness this summer, so leaving one or two spots open for an occasion like this was a tad easier to navigate for the sport compared to football.

But even then, being in this spot of pure legal chaos was on the mind of plenty, including the NCAA.

The mind-boggling part of this entire saga is that attorneys, like Ryan Downton, essentially told the NCAA this was coming.

When former Vanderbilt linebacker Langston Patterson sued the organization in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee over the amount of years athletes are allowed to participate in college athletics, the warning shot to the NCAA was clearly given.

"We asked the NCAA to give everyone five years last year when we filed the Patterson lawsuit. They said no," Ryan Downton told OutKick-FOX News. "Now they’ve done it, but excluded the athletes asking for the change.  It feels like the NCAA is saying, ‘you had a good idea, but we can’t let you enjoy the benefits of it.’ Just like they changed the name. We called it ‘five-for-five.’ They call it ‘age-based eligibility.’  It’s the same thing, but the NCAA tries to pretend it isn’t."

I've seen a few public relations' nightmares over the years that involve the NCAA, but this summer has been one for the ages. But, they cannot stop fighting these lawsuits, no matter how many are filed against them.

Why? Well that comes down to the organization actually granting a blanket-waiver themselves, and then having thousands of athletes gain an additional year of eligibility with nowhere to go. The NCAA might not want to admit it, but they are most likely in this for the long haul, though not for the reasons you might think at first.

Lost in the noise surrounding each statement from the NCAA desperately pleading for Congress to pass legislation that would provide some type of antitrust cover that keeps them out of courtrooms, is the fact that if they would have at least 'grandfathered' in the 2022 class with this new eligibility rule, they most certainly would not have their own lawyers racking up frequent-flyer miles on a consistent basis.

TRUMP ADVISOR, EX-NFL PLAYER CODY CAMPBELL WARNS PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT IS FINAL CHANCE TO RESTORE ORDER

"The NCAA is fighting tooth and nail to stop my clients from playing this year. Meanwhile, the NCAA is intensely lobbying Congress to pass the PCSA," plaintiff attorney Ryan Downton told OutKick-FOX News. "The irony is that if the PCSA (Protect College Sports Act) became law today, all of my clients become immediately eligible and get to play this year.  

"The NCAA is like a referee who thinks he’s bigger than the game he’s officiating - just do the right thing and get out of the way."

From courtrooms to Zoom hearings that allow attorneys to appear before multiple judges in a single day if needed, much of the current chaos feels entirely self-inflicted. And, that would most likely be the easiest way to comprehend one side of this fight.

Plaintiffs (athletes) are going at the NCAA in multiple courtrooms, in multiple states, arguing that if the new five-and-five rule was being implemented, then athletes who exhausted their clock this past season under the old rule should be granted the same rights that players under the new guidelines are utilizing.

NCAA Rocked By Colorado Judge's 2022 Class Eligibility Ruling That Could Reshape College Sports This Year

And then came U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney of Colorado, who granted a bombshell injunction in the [Wisne v. NCAA] class action lawsuit that has now sent the college athletics world into further chaos. That was filed by former Northern Colorado men's basketball player Brock Wisne.

This meant that athletes across all sports were given a blanket waiver to compete this season, if they had a year of eligibility left to use as part of the 2022 class. These rulings are not just being used in basketball, even if the sport is garnering most of the headlines.

In some states, like Tennessee and Ohio, injunctions granted in those cases will allow players who were plaintiffs in the lawsuits to utilize the transfer portal. But, in the Colorado case, the plaintiffs are not being granted an additional portal window.

"This is one of those situations where the facts really drive a lot of the story," Associate professor at Boise State's College of Business and Economics, Sam Ehrlich told OutKick-FOX News. "The law has already been winning on a lot of these eligibility rule cases, but judges are really resonating with the idea that these players in particular are being put in a bad spot -- having to compete against guys who played five or six years and the players after them getting five.

"It feels fundamentally unfair to judges who look for even treatment, and I think that drives a lot of the legal conclusions too, especially since the legal theories are all about whether the treatment is arbitrary or unfair."

In reality, if the NCAA were to now just give in, and grant blanket waivers on their own, then they'd be admitting fault while also opening the floodgates to thousands of athletes who would be eligible, but have nowhere to play this season.

So, whether they like spending the money and resources or not, the NCAA has to continue fighting these cases in courtrooms across the country.

On Tuesday, Indiana announced that star defensive lineman Stephen Daley, who was injured in a postgame celebration following the 2025 Big Ten championship, was returning for the 2026 season by way of the court ruling in Colorado.

"If it all works out and he can participate and help this football team, then his life could change," Curt Cignetti said about Daley returning. "I know one thing about him, he’ll give it his best shot, he really will, and we’ll just see what happens."

College Football Is Finally Back After Months Of NCAA Lawsuits, NIL Drama And Congressional Fights

That line from Cignetti on how Indiana will 'see what happens' mainly centers around the NCAA appealing the Colorado court's decision.

If the organization is awarded an 'administrative stay', then the injunction would be lifted while proceedings continue and the rules would go back in place, meaning Stephen Daley would be ineligible once again.

But, who's to say the Indiana lineman wouldn’t then file a lawsuit in state court?

The other problem for NCAA officials, and lawyers, is that there is no end in sight. Whether it's athletes suing for an additional year or monetary damages they feel are owed for the organizations misdoings, this is not slowing down any time soon.

And one of the most interesting parts of this entire ordeal centers around the fact that if Congress were to pass the 'Protect College Sports Act', I don't know if there's enough antitrust protection wrapped in this legislation to keep them out of court in the future.

Don't worry though, it will all get sorted out and cooler heads will prevail.

Right?

item.title: Dem senator presses OpenAI, Anthropic for answers in AI hacking probe
item.description: Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester demands security logs and transcripts from OpenAI and Anthropic after AI agents allegedly hacked third parties during testing.
item.content:encoded:
Revelations of OpenAI and Anthropic artificial intelligence agents hacking third parties has drawn the "serious concern" of Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, D-Del., who is now seeking answers from the two businesses incorporated as public benefit companies (PBC) in her state.

In separate letters dated Thursday to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, viewed by Fox News Digital, Blunt Rochester has requested detailed timelines, model instructions, internal approvals, security logs and complete transcripts from the companies’ cyber evaluations.

The member of the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee gave both companies until Sept. 6 to respond.

AI KILL SWITCH BILL COULD SHUT DOWN ROGUE MODELS

"These incidents mark the first publicly confirmed instances of a frontier AI model autonomously launching unauthorized attacks on real people and companies, underscoring the urgent need for federal oversight of frontier AI systems," Blunt Rochester wrote to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, calling for federal testing standards, containment rules and disclosure requirements for evaluations of powerful AI systems.

Her concern follows another letter Monday, as first reported by Fox News Digital, from a coalition of 15 red-state attorneys general warning Altman to preserve documents and halt certain high-risk cybersecurity tests after an experimental artificial intelligence agent allegedly escaped a controlled environment and carried out a multi-day hack into outside computer systems.

One day later, the United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute (AISI) identified 19 cases in which AI agents took actions outside the authorized scope of testing. Two involved OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, while 17 involved Anthropic’s Mythos 5.

OPENAI'S SAM ALTMAN WANTS TO NEGOTIATE A 5% STAKE IN COMPANY FOR US IF COMPETITORS AGREE TO KEY PROVISION

"Anthropic models’ repeated attacks on third parties with no knowledge of, or role in, Anthropic and AISI’s evaluations demonstrate an alarming pattern of malicious behavior," Blunt Rochester's letter to Amodei read. "Furthermore, the successful attempts by these models to gain unauthorized internet access across multiple sandbox testing environments meant to be cut off from the public internet highlight serious issues with Anthropic’s testing partnerships and procedures.

READ THE AISI REPORT – APP USERS, CLICK HERE:

"To be clear, 'misunderstanding[s]' and 'misconfiguration[s]' with sandbox partners are unacceptable when the stakes are this high.

"We cannot wait for a more consequential incident before establishing federal testing standards, containment requirements, and disclosure obligations for frontier model evaluations.

"Left unaddressed, these gaps could allow a future model, potentially one with greater capability or less oversight, to compromise critical infrastructure, financial systems, or sensitive data."

These investigations carry a distinct Delaware dimension: OpenAI and Anthropic are organized as Delaware PBCs — legal structures that allow them to operate for profit but require their directors to weigh more than shareholder returns.

KARR BLUETOOTH FLAW EXPOSES 2.2M CARS TO THEFT RISK

Under Delaware law, a PBC board must balance three things: its stockholders' financial interests, the interests of people materially affected by the company's conduct and the specific public benefit written into the company's charter.

READ THE LETTER TO OPENAI – APP USERS, CLICK HERE:

"This incident marks an important moment for AI safety and we take the questions raised by the Attorneys General seriously," OpenAI wrote in a statement to Fox News Digital after Monday's letter from the state AGs.

"We are conducting a thorough review along with external advisors and with oversight from the Safety and Security Committee of the Board of Directors. Once the review is complete, we will share a technical report with the Attorneys General and other relevant government authorities and publish our findings publicly."

Blunt Rochester wants records related to the AI agent hacking now, too.

CLICKLOCK MAC MALWARE LOCKS APPS UNTIL YOU GIVE IN

"I appreciate that OpenAI has published preliminary findings, is coordinating with third parties on remediation, and is reviewing its approach to model testing," she wrote to Altman, adding to Amodei, "I appreciate Anthropic’s voluntary review of its cybersecurity evaluations and public disclosure of the findings, and I encourage other companies to follow suit.

"However, these incidents demonstrate the potential risks of deploying pre-release models internally, particularly when safeguards are reduced, even when strictly for testing and evaluation," she wrote to both CEOs.

READ THE LETTER TO ANTHROPIC – APP USERS, CLICK HERE:

OpenAI disclosed in July that GPT-5.6 Sol and an internal prototype escaped an internal sandbox while their normal cybersecurity restrictions were disabled. The models allegedly accessed Hugging Face's database and other services, launched roughly 17,000 attacks, used stolen credentials and exploited at least one previously unknown vulnerability.

A separate test conducted by contractor Irregular allegedly allowed an OpenAI model onto the public internet because of a configuration error. The model mistook a real website for a target in a simulated hacking challenge and exploited a live security vulnerability.

"AISI identified 19 instances in which an agent took unsanctioned action beyond the scope of the evaluation. Seventeen of the 19 instances involved Anthropic’s Mythos 5; two involved OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol," Blunt Rochester wrote.

The institute’s most serious findings included an agent attempting to place malicious code into a widely used open-source project on GitHub, creating fake identities to pressure a human maintainer, contacting real people and leaving public instructions that other AI systems could use to continue the operation. The maintainer rejected the code, and investigators reported finding no resulting real-world harm.

PAIDWORK BREACH EXPOSES 23M USER RECORDS

Blunt Rochester’s Anthropic letter separately cites three incidents in which Claude models allegedly gained unauthorized internet access and attacked three undisclosed organizations during cyber evaluations conducted with standard safeguards disabled.

Two of the Anthropic models reportedly recognized that they had reached the open internet and were interacting with real targets but continued their attacks.

"It is particularly concerning that Anthropic’s first identified security breach dates back to April 2026 and was not identified until three months later," Blunt Rochester wrote to Amodei.

"This is precisely the kind of emergent, autonomous behavior and offensive cyber capability that Congress, the intelligence community, and experts have repeatedly warned could outpace existing safeguards and could pose a severe threat to the safety and security of all Americans," she added in both letters.

FOX NEWS POLL: MOVE OVER BIG BROTHER, VOTERS SEE BIG TECH AS GREATER THREAT TO US

The requested records go beyond basic incident reports. Blunt Rochester is seeking the prompts and full instructions given to the models, time-stamped accounts of how the breaches unfolded, the identities or positions of officials authorized to reduce safety controls and an explanation of why automated monitoring did not immediately detect and stop the activity.

She also asked whether federal agencies were notified, whether the companies are confident they discovered the full extent of the unauthorized access and whether previous incidents went unreported.

Blunt Rochester has a federal oversight basis for pursuing the information. She represents the state whose corporate law governs both companies and is the ranking Democrat on the Senate's Science, Manufacturing and Competitiveness Subcommittee, which has jurisdiction over oversight of science and technology research, development and policy.

Her position does not make her Delaware’s corporate regulator — that role falls principally to state officials and courts — and the companies’ PBC status does not automatically give a U.S. senator access to their internal files.

Blunt Rochester could, however, use the companies’ responses — or a refusal to respond — to press for hearings, legislation or committee-level compulsory action.

"Given the significance of this incident, transparency with Congress is essential to ensure that the oversight and safety frameworks governing increasingly autonomous, cyber-capable AI systems keep pace with their capabilities," Blunt Rochester's letters concluded.

Fox News Digital reached out to Altman and Amodei for comment on Blunt Rochester's requests Thursday morning.

item.title: Unearthed paper exposes Dem House hopeful's 'insane' proposal for meeting climate goals
item.description: Manny Rutinel's resurfaced paper argued governments should incentivize ranchers to transition to plant-based farming in Colorado's top cattle district.
item.content:encoded:
Manny Rutinel, Democratic candidate for Congress in Colorado's 8th Congressional District, once co-authored a paper that argued that livestock — not fossil fuels — should be more of a focus to combat global warming.

"Simply put, achieving the Paris Agreement goals will be nearly impossible without ambitious policies that reform our food system," Rutinel wrote in a 2022 paper with the Environmental Law Institute.

"Despite the growing awareness of animal agriculture’s climate impact, climate policy and action have historically focused on electricity and fuel use."

EUROPE'S 'GREEN IDEOLOGY' CLIMATE AGENDA RISKS CRUSHING ITS INDUSTRY, ENVIRONMENT MINISTER WARNS

The resurfaced paper is just the most recent resurfaced content complicating the political calculus for Rutinel as he strives to convince voters that his past rhetoric on climate and farming is not fully representative of his views now.

Four years since the publication of his work, Rutinel's election very well could depend on the heavy ranching presence in his district.

Colorado’s 8th district is Colorado’s leading producer of beef cattle and dairy, accounting for 26% of the state’s output, according to Upstate Colorado Economic Development. Of its 2.5 million acres, 75% are devoted to farming and raising livestock.

In recent months, Rutinel has worked to convince voters that he recognizes the industry's importance.

"Like all industry, there are bad apples, and I’ve spoken out against those bad apples that cause extreme and unnecessary animal cruelty in parts of the food industry and against the environmental cost of unsustainable food practices," he said.

"They’re good stewards of the land, they care for their animals, and they are the backbone of our economy and our communities. Colorado ranchers are my friends and neighbors, and I’ve gotten to know them," he added.

BATTLEGROUND DEMOCRAT FLIP-FLOPS ON CONVERSION THERAPY AFTER LEFT-WING BACKLASH

But through advocacy in college, testimony made before local government and a climate group he started, Rutinel has pressed the case that many climate advocates have articulated in the past: that livestock contribute to global emissions as a byproduct through their digestive systems.

The resurfaced paper brings a government-led approach to many of his vocalized positions.

In it, Rutinel argued that ranchers and animal farmers should be incentivized through government initiatives to transition to plant-based farming with either a carrot or a stick.

"Governments can require that agribusiness internalize the environmental, public health, and animal welfare costs of animal farms through regulations, mandates or taxes," Rutinel wrote, suggesting penalties for companies to make up for their production.

"But one food system policy idea has not received sufficient attention: the direct funding of farm transitions from concentrated animal feeding operations to plant-based operations," he added.

Rutinel also argued state and local governments could finance offsetting projects that would reduce emissions.

"For example, a manufacturing facility in California can decrease its net emissions by purchasing offset credits that finance a reforestation project in Brazil. Offset credits can be purchased voluntarily or to exceed emission allowances within a compliance market."

To some onlookers who have cast doubt on Rutinel's positions in the past, the statements appear to confirm that his position is further left on energy than many Democrats pushing aggressive climate initiatives through legislation like the Green New Deal.

"You have to be legitimately insane to look at the Green New Deal and think it doesn't go far enough. Meatless Manny's vision to ban ranching would not only lead to catastrophic job losses in Colorado but also cause a beef shortage across America," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

HOUSE REPUBLICANS SPLINTER OVER PESTICIDE PROVISION IN FARM BILL AS MAHA MOVEMENT FLEXES ITS MUSCLE

Rutinel’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether he continues to believe that climate reform must, on some level, mean change for farming industries.

Having cleared the Democratic primary, Rutinel will face off against Rep. Gabe Evans in the state’s Nov. 3, 2026, general election.

item.title: Dannon's decision to kill beloved yogurt sparks fan revolt: 'It's what I got out of bed for'
item.description: Dannon coffee yogurt fans launched a petition and flooded social media after the beloved flavor was discontinued, but the company hints at a return.
item.content:encoded:
Dannon's coffee-flavored yogurt earned a cult-like following over the decades. Now that it's disappeared from store shelves, longtime devotees have launched a petition to bring it back, flooded social media with disappointment and searched for substitutes.

"In an unexpected move, Dannon recently discontinued their much-loved coffee yogurt flavor as of April 1," reads a Change.org petition urging Dannon to bring back coffee yogurt.

"This has left countless fans of this unique and delicious product in dismay. Coffee yogurt provided a delightful blend of rich coffee flavor and creamy yogurt, a perfect option for those seeking a pick-me-up in a healthy and satisfying snack."

DISCONTINUED CRACKER BARREL FOODS THAT FANS ARE BEGGING TO GET BACK

A 5.3-ounce cup of Dannon's coffee yogurt, known by enthusiasts as simply "DCY," "contained about 32 milligrams of caffeine, or about a third of an 8-ounce cup of coffee," along with 11 grams of added sugar, The Wall Street Journal reported.

New Jersey lawyer Doron Zeif ate DCY for 40 years and told the publication, "It's what I got out of bed for."

Lisa Signorelli, a retiree from New York, told the Journal she frequently bought cases of DCY to feed her "50-year obsession."

"Discontinuing this flavor has removed a valuable and cherished option for yogurt lovers everywhere, particularly for those who appreciate the distinct taste of coffee," the petition further states.

Social media users echoed the petition's sentiment.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"I'm going through serious withdrawal symptoms now that Dannon has discontinued their coffee yogurt, which I have been happily eating for years and years," one person wrote on a Reddit forum asking if it's possible to make something "akin to Dannon coffee yogurt."

"I'm honestly quite bummed about it," the user added. "I know there are other companies out there that make coffee yogurt, but it's the texture that was a big part of it."

"I'm seriously going through withdrawal!" another Reddit user commented. "Other coffee yogurts are not the same. And making our own version, while healthier, would also not taste the same. I have been having this particular Dannon for literally decades, every day!"

Several people offered advice for replicating the fan-favorite yogurt by adding instant or liquid coffee to other Dannon yogurts. One commenter encouraged fans of Dannon's coffee yogurt to call the company, noting, "A human being actually picks up the phone!"

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

The Dannon Coffee Yogurt Fanatics Facebook page includes many people exchanging methods for trying to match the DCY flavor.

"I was a serial DCY user for some 40 years, and I was convinced I'd never get over Dannon's decision this year," wrote a woman who identified herself as a "recovering fanatic." "I tried DIY DCY, but none made the cut. My son-in-law convinced me to try Icelandic Provisions Cold Brew Coffee Skyr, and within days I was hooked. DCY would seem too sweet and thin by comparison."

The door doesn't seem to be completely shut forever to Dannon's coffee yogurt, however.

"Dannon coffee yogurt will come back in ways that reflect the taste preferences, flavor profile and nutritional benefits many consumers seek in the yogurt aisle today," Rafael Acevedo, president of Dannon's yogurt division, told the Journal.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

A post on Dannon's Instagram shows a photo of DCY and says, "Miss it? We'd love to hear from you." Dannon captioned the post, "The passion for Dannon coffee yogurt has been incredible to see. DM us and we will keep you posted for future updates."

"My grandmother, who passed away in 2011, had one every day," one user replied. "It was a treat when she'd share it with me as a kid, and now it serves as a special memory. It's also the best flavor! Please bring it back!"

"I miss it so much!" wrote another. "Please bring it back; I am tired of mixing coffee and vanilla yours from other brands. It never tastes as good as the classic Dannon coffee."

Dannon declined to comment to Fox News Digital.

item.title: Fetterman answers whether he'll cross the aisle to confirm Trump AG nominee Todd Blanche
item.description: John Fetterman says he won't vote for Todd Blanche as attorney general, breaking from his pattern of often supporting Trump's DOJ and Cabinet picks.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said Wednesday he would not vote for acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to officially take over the role leading the Department of Justice.

During a Wednesday appearance on comedian Jon Stewart's podcast, Fetterman was pressed on Democrats' failure to use the Senate filibuster to block President Donald Trump's Cabinet nominees. The senator responded by claiming he would not vote for Blanche, who is Trump's choice for attorney general.

"Many of them I didn't vote for," Fetterman said, referring to Trump's Cabinet nominees.

JOHN FETTERMAN MAKES IT 'VERY CLEAR' THAT HE'S 'NOT GOING TO BE A REPUBLICAN' DESPITE DEM BACKLASH

"And if you're going to bring up Blanche, I'm not going to vote for him as well. There are some that I would vote for, and then there are many that I haven't because I just don't believe that's the right person for the job overall. I really try to call balls and strikes," he told Stewart.

Fetterman has been one of the Democratic senators most supportive of Trump's Cabinet nominees, voting "yea" to confirm half of his nominees, according to a Fox News Digital review.

He was the only Democrat to support Trump's previous choice for attorney general, Pam Bondi. He also helped push Markwayne Mullin, the newest Homeland Security secretary, over the line, casting the decisive vote to advance Mullin out of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, 8-7. Fetterman was again the only Democrat to vote for Mullin's confirmation, joining the 53 Senate Republicans to confirm Mullin in a 54-37 vote.

Despite Fetterman supporting Trump's previous pick to head the Department of Justice, it appears the president will not be able to count on his vote this time around.

TRUMP AG PICK TODD BLANCHE FACES SENATE TEST IN FIRST MAJOR CONFIRMATION FIGHT SINCE GRAHAM’S DEATH

Bondi won her nomination from the Senate in a 54-46 vote. Todd Blanche will likely have at least two fewer votes than that tally, as Fetterman joins Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, in publicly expressing opposition to Blanche.

"Mr. Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation," Collins said Tuesday.

Collins notably voted to confirm Blanche as the assistant attorney general in March.

Two other potential GOP holdouts – Sens. Bill Cassidy, R-La., and Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, – are still undecided, according to The Hill.

A pair of Republicans who had previously opposed Blanche's nomination – Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C. – flipped to "yeas" after Blanche agreed to stop pursuing a planned anti-weaponization fund.

The Senate Judiciary Committee voted to advance Blanche's nomination to the full Senate on a strict party line vote, 12-10.

Fox News Digital contacted the White House, the DOJ and Fetterman for further comment.

item.title: Trump told donors 'we need to elect JD,' source confirms, as he weighs Vance or Rubio in 2028
item.description: President Donald Trump told Republican donors "we need to elect JD" in a private Oval Office meeting, a source confirmed to Fox News Digital.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump has publicly been coy about whether he might back Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio to succeed him in the White House, but private comments to donors suggest he might be leaning toward the man he already picked as his running mate in 2024.

"At the end of the day, we need to elect JD," Trump said during an Oval Office meeting with donors roughly two weeks ago, a source with knowledge of the comments, who asked to remain anonymous to speak more freely, confirmed to Fox News Digital.

The news was first reported by The Washington Post.

While Vance remains the clear hypothetical frontrunner, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has narrowed the gap in national polls and surveys conducted in key early voting presidential primary states, as well as in Republican straw polls, ahead of a race that is not expected to begin in earnest until after this autumn's midterm elections.

VANCE, CRUZ, HEAD TO IOWA ON 2026 MISSIONS AS 2028 GOP RACE TO SUCCEED TRUMP HEATS UP

While Post sources say the remark is not evidence Trump has made a choice between his VP or Rubio, a man he has handed many hats in his administration, it is a rare and previously unreported lean of his long-term thinking.

Trump made just one reference to Vance in his donor speech in Las Vegas on Wednesday night, hailing "the war on fraud led by our great Vice President JD Vance: He's doing a great job."

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Vance's office for comment Thursday morning.

Rubio, who as a senator from Florida was one of more than a dozen GOP contenders who ran and lost to Trump in the 2016 presidential primary, came in a close second to Vance earlier this year in the closely watched 2028 Republican presidential nomination straw poll at the annual Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC).

The latest surveys and straw poll results are fuel for intrigue over what some in the Republican Party see as a budding rivalry between Rubio and Vance, who describe each other as friends.

"The president runs this administration: He is the very top of the administration; he makes orders," Vance told "The Ingraham Angle" in an exclusive sit down Wednesday night. "We, of course, have debates and conversations about what exactly we should do, but when the president of the United States makes a decision, we’re unified in this administration in carrying out that mission."

Despite Vance having won the 2024 running mate sweepstakes, Trump has also lavishly praised Rubio for his work in peacemaking efforts in Venezuela, Cuba and the Middle East, while simultaneously serving as national security advisor among his many leadership roles in the administration.

The president earlier this year declared that Rubio would go down as "the greatest secretary of state in history."

Trump has also promoted a Vance-Rubio ticket as "unstoppable" — stopping short of explicitly saying who should be at the top of the ticket.

Trump did say last year that Vance is "most likely" his heir, because "in all fairness, he's the vice president."

NEW POLL COMPLICATES VANCE’S STATUS AS TRUMP’S LIKELY 2028 HEIR APPARENT

Trump joked at the White House Correspondents Dinner last month – rescheduled after dodging another assassination attempt earlier this spring – he would be running for president for a fourth in a troll to his critics, donning a Trump 2028

While Vance has demurred when questioned about 2028, he has built a political team of advisors who, if he runs as expected, would quickly build out a presidential campaign.

Rubio, who is crisscrossing the globe, does not have a similar group of political aides, and Rubio has said he will back Vance if the vice president launches a 2028 campaign.

Notably, Vance is the RNC's finance chair, ostensibly giving him the keys to the cash vault of more than $128 million cash on hand, according to the June Federal Elections Commission filing.

"Vice President Vance has been a fundraising powerhouse for the RNC, supercharging our war chest as we head into the midterms," RNC Chair Joe Gruters told Fox News Digital in a statement. "He’s held record-breaking events across the country and brought new and longtime donors together with his ability to connect every corner of the America First movement. 

"As we prepare to protect and expand our Republican majorities, Vice President Vance will be a driving force behind the resources, energy, and momentum needed to win."

Republican sources confirmed to Fox News earlier this year that a group of GOP donors supporting the secretary of state is quietly exploring ways to boost Rubio's political profile, which has not sat well with some in the president's political orbit.

VANCE CONFRONTED ABOUT 2028 AMBITIONS AFTER TRUMP TEASES 'DREAM TEAM' RUBIO TICKET

"Vice President Vance is the future of the Republican Party, and Marco Rubio is one of his closest friends in the administration," an operative in Trump's political orbit told Fox News Digital earlier this year.

"The divisive stories from some donors trying to cause chaos are not helpful," the operative, who asked to remain anonymous to speak more freely, emphasized.

Trump more recently questioned White House staff about the two possible contenders during a flight aboard Marine One, according to the Post. Although one adviser told the newspaper that Trump has privately settled on Vance as the Republican heir apparent, six other advisers and allies said they were not convinced that the president had made up his mind.

Those advisers noted that Trump sometimes gives different signals to different audiences and could change his position before the 2028 campaign begins. His aides also broadly expect him to delay any formal endorsement, in part to avoid diminishing his own influence during the remainder of his presidency.

DEMOCRATS BUILD MIDTERM MOMENTUM, BUT REPUBLICANS STILL IN DRIVER'S SEAT IN SENATE MAJORITY BATTLE

The dynamic resembles Trump’s 2024 search for a running mate, when Vance and Rubio were among the finalists. Advisers told the Post that Trump enjoys maintaining suspense around major political decisions and is reluctant to hand the spotlight to a potential successor too early.

Vance admitted to Ingraham it is his "job" to take criticism, particularly if absorbs pressure from the president. 

"It’s my job, Laura," Vance said. "If the worst thing that happens is I take flak for the president to make his administration more successful, I’ll be happy about that."

Vance did not talk about whether he will run. 

He did say in June that he planned to discuss his political future with his wife after the midterm elections and has maintained that he remains focused on serving as vice president.

People close to Vance previously told the Post that he intended to wait until after the birth of his fourth child before seriously considering a campaign. The child was born July 19.

The 2026 midterms could shape the emerging succession contest. Republican losses could encourage additional candidates to enter the race and make it easier for them to criticize Trump’s administration or challenge his preferred successor. A strong performance, by contrast, could strengthen Trump’s ability to shape the 2028 field.

Vance has spent much of his vice presidency building relationships with Republican donors and activists. He is closely associated with the younger, populist wing of the MAGA coalition and has taken on political and policy assignments that have helped raise his profile.

Rubio historically has had stronger ties to traditional Republican donors, while Vance has deeper support among the party’s newer populist base.

item.title: Women's advocacy leader asks 'why have a WNBA if we're going to allow guys in' amid trans debate
item.description: American Heritage Girls founder praises Sophie Cunningham's courage on trans athletes while expressing disappointment in Caitlin Clark's silence.
item.content:encoded:
Sophie Cunningham is grabbing the attention of women's advocacy groups.

Patti Garibay founded American Heritage Girls in 1993 as a way to keep faith in the Girl Scout mission, but as she feels biological girls' and women's safe spaces have been taken over by biological men, she now has a new goal in mind.

"There's so much confusion around it. What were traditionally safe spaces and places for women are no longer safe spaces and places," Garibay said in a recent interview with Fox News Digital. "And now parents, even when they're calling our office asking about potentially bringing their daughter into American Heritage Girls, the question is about policies, membership policies, and are you biologically female, or do you allow others in, because all of the other organizations, youth organizations are now allowing boys that say that they feel like they're girls into these intimate spaces and places, such as the cabin at the camp or the locker room at the sports team.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"These are of grave concerns to parents because they want those safe places for their daughters to be able to really thrive, not worry about competition of biological male against them."

The issue has now gone well into the sports conversation, and Garibay is wondering, "Why have a WNBA if we're going to allow guys in?"

That's why Garibay felt a sigh of relief when Cunningham showed her support for keeping trans athletes out of biological girls' sports.

"I think Sophie has had great courage and that is what we teach American Heritage Girls to have, to have courage to stand up for what's right and not worry so much about the potential loss that's involved because when you do the right thing, you are rewarded in different ways," Garibay said, while admitting she was "disappointed" that Caitlin Clark did not directly address it when recently asked.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SEES SUPPORT SURGE AFTER STAR PUTS CAREER ON LINE FOR GIRLS SPORTS

"I felt like that was a little bit of a concern. Probably her handlers suggested that she avoid that at all costs. Sophie, on the other hand, has decided to get into the miry waters of this and to stand for what I believe is truth."

Garibay, though, is adamant that there are "lots of opportunities" for trans youth to be included.

"There's so many other opportunities for them to be able to find those places. And I do think perhaps they, just like I had to start American Heritage Girls, perhaps there's something that they can start too that they would feel very good about being amongst themselves and have that support that they so need to address the mental health issues that come along with all of it. It's very positive to have friends and to have allies around you," Garibay said.

"We've been fighting this fight since back in getting rights to vote for goodness sake. This has been going on a long time. Why are we going backwards?"

item.title: Shaq pours cold water on WNBA's gambling post, reflects on players' 'professional jealousy' of Caitlin Clark
item.description: Shaquille O'Neal weighed in on the Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers wager the "professional jealousy" Caitlin Clark has faced in the WNBA.
item.content:encoded:
The WNBA has been under critical fire since the first day Caitlin Clark joined the league.

While being in the midst of culture war battles, Clark has also been the victim of some hard fouls due to what's commonly been perceived as massive jealousy from her peers.

As the WNBA has dealt with its own apparent battle amid its players on different sides of the transgender athlete debate, the league drummed up even more controversy after deleting a post about a wager between Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

The two stars recorded a video in which they wagered $400 on a recent game between their respective teams — betting of any kind is strictly prohibited under the WNBA's new collective bargaining agreement, with Section 5 of Article 14 in the agreement dedicated to gambling regulations. A WNBA spokesperson released a statement on Thursday claiming that the quickly deleted video was "intended to be lighthearted," but that it "simply missed the mark."

NBA legend Shaquille O'Neal, though, saw practically nothing wrong with what Reese and Bueckers did.

SHAQUILLE O'NEAL TALKS LEBRON JAMES' LAKERS LEGACY, WHY HIS NEW 76ERS MIGHT BE EXTREMELY 'DANGEROUS'

"That’s what we call a 'homeboy bet.' If it falls under gambling, it would be under the misdemeanor section; people need to stop it. She's not f---ing point shaving," O'Neal told Fox News Digital recently.

The former big man also admitted that there is "professional jealousy" when it comes to Clark, but "it’s what we call the rites of passage."

"There's girls that are going, 'You don't talk about me like that, you talk about her.' You gotta take advantage of that opportunity. You have to go at who they think the best is. If you got other people coming at her, then it is what it is. Once she gets through this next year and keeps playing the way she's playing, they’ll have no choice but to love and accept it," O'Neal said. "But this is what we call rites of passage. We don’t just let youngsters come in and take over because they’re getting all the props from the media.

"Caitlin's a tough cookie. She'll be able to get over it. Angel's throwing 'bows, talking smack, letting everyone know, 'I'm not scared.' Caitlin's probably gotta do a little more of that."

Clark recently went after the WNBA, saying it needs to do a better job of protecting its players both on and off the court.

OutKick's Mark Harris contributed to this report.

item.title: Fauci held in contempt as COVID cellphone lands in hands of Senate investigators
item.description: Sen. Rand Paul's committee voted to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he invoked the Fifth Amendment more than 100 times at his hearing.
item.content:encoded:
Senate Republicans moved to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress in their pursuit of forcing the former architect of the nation’s COVID-19 response to go on record about his actions leading up to and during the pandemic.

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted on sharp party lines to charge Fauci, the former chief medical advisor to the president, with contempt after he refused to answer questions from both sides of the aisle over fear of self-incrimination.

The move follows Fauci’s decision to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights more than 100 times during his hearing last week, which prompted the panel’s chair, Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., to vow that he would face "repercussions" for not testifying, or at least how Paul envisioned.

FAUCI'S HHS IPHONE TURNED OVER TO SENATE INVESTIGATORS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

Typically, once a contempt resolution passes by committee, it heads to the Senate floor for a full vote. However, Paul’s resolution allows that step to be skipped altogether and allows him to send the referral directly to the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia.

But Paul wants the Department of Justice (DOJ) involved as soon as possible. There’s also the question whether Fauci’s pardon from former President Joe Biden protected him during the hearing, which Paul hopes to find answers to.

"It’s a good legal discussion, and we will make those legal points to DOJ in sending the referral over," Paul told Fox News Digital ahead of the hearing.

RAND PAUL PREDICTS FAUCI CONTEMPT VOTE WILL PASS, VOWS SWIFT DOJ REFERRAL

It’s another chapter in the feud between Paul and Fauci that has extended over the last several years since the onset of the pandemic.

Paul has accused the former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) director of funding "risky" research that led to an alleged lab leak of the COVID-19 virus in China and has demanded that he end up behind bars.

And in the background, a copy of Fauci’s pandemic-era cellphone is now in the possession of Senate Republican investigators.

Fox News Digital confirmed that the Robert F. Kennedy Jr.-led Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) sent over a copy of the phone to the Senate Homeland Security Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations chaired by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

TOP 5 MOMENTS FROM FAUCI'S HEARING: PAUL BOOTS LAWYER, MORENO ERUPTS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

That committee falls under the umbrella of Paul’s Homeland Security panel, which also received a trove of over 1,000 pages of Fauci’s personal diary before last week’s hearing.

It is unclear if Johnson and Paul have access to the information on the phone.

Meanwhile, across the marble expanse of the Capitol, Republican investigators in the House are cooking up their own probe into Fauci.

House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., previously signaled that he was not done with Fauci, either.

After the longtime public health official pleaded the Fifth Amendment during his Senate hearing, Comer questioned the validity of his preemptive pardon granted by President Joe Biden. He also said his committee would be questioning Fauci further, though he did not elaborate.

"If former President Biden’s blanket autopen pardon is valid, then Dr. Fauci has no right to refuse to answer questions," Comer said, noting his committee had done extensive work probing the autopen pardons. "Based on the release of Dr. Fauci’s diary, which should have been provided to the House Oversight Committee last Congress...we’ll be asking Dr. Fauci whether he stands by his previous testimony to our Committee."

item.title: Social media explodes as WNBA star Kelsey Plum leaps into the arms of opposing coach during play
item.description: Kelsey Plum barreled into opposing coach Karl Smesko's arms during the Phoenix-Atlanta game, and social media could not stop talking about the moment.
item.content:encoded:
Another night, and another "Only in the WNBA" moment. Thankfully, this one had nothing to do with racism, men playing women's sports, or Angel Reese missing a 2-foot layup.

Nope. This one was just some good, clean family fun from last night's Phoenix-Atlanta game.

For those who missed it (and that's literally all of you), the Dream took down the Mercury, 96-82, in a back-and-forth contest. Reese finished with 14 points and 10 assists.

ANGEL REESE PUT UP ONE OF THE WORST BASKETBALL SHOTS OF ALL TIME, AND THEN SOMETHING AMAZING HAPPENED

But I don't care about the Xs and Os of last night's game. What I care about is what transpired late in the game, when Kelsey Plum went barreling down the court, veered too much to the bench, and ended up in the arms of opposing coach, Karl Smesko.

You're simply not getting this sort of content out of the NBA, folks.

Soak it all in:

What a scene. What a moment.

What a league!

Every night, it's something new. Most of it's ... not great ... but it's still a talker, and that's all that matters. Yesterday Sophie Cunningham went on some long rant about how WNBA beat reporters don't ever talk about basketball.

Of course not, Sophie! The basketball ain't what makes the WNBA compelling. Sure, some of the games are good, but most of them are terrible. The officiating is terrible. The matchups are terrible.

WNBA COACH TORCHES LEAGUE’S OFFICIATING AFTER LATEST BIZARRE NO-CALL: ‘IT’S A F------ JOKE’

We want to break down the other stuff. Stuff like Kelsey Plum leaping into a coach's arms and putting all of her faith into him.

Stuff like Angel Reese saying black Barbie dolls didn't exist until the 2000s.

Stuff like Caitlin Clark getting mugged with no foul being called, or Sophie Cunningham pointing at some obnoxious player, or ESPN drooling over a coach wearing a pro-trans shirt.

THAT's the stuff that gets eyeballs. Fair or not, it's a fact. It's the truth.

Plum, by the way, had a monster game last night. She finished with 19 points, five rebounds and four assists. Good for her.

All social media could talk about, however, was the leap. I get it.

Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham does not believe that female athletes should have to share a locker room or compete against biological males.

For simply protecting women's sports and young girls, the eight-year WNBA veteran has received tremendous pushback from many in the media and recently addressed the fallout that feels like it may never fully end.

Cunningham joined USA Network's WNBA broadcast on Wednesday evening, certainly knowing she would be asked about her opposition to transgender athletes competing in women's sports and the pushback that has come along with that.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM DOUBLES DOWN AHEAD OF SUN GAME AFTER ESPN PROFILE STIRS CONTROVERSY: 'I SAID WHAT I SAID'

Elle Duncan, formerly of ESPN, didn't want to revisit "the actual issue that brought us to this point" during her conversation with Cunningham, but instead asked her specifically about the WNBA's suspension of Seattle Storm minority owner Celeste Keaton.

Keaton allegedly called a pair of teenage Sophie Cunningham fans "f---ing insane" during Indiana's win in Seattle on July 28. Duncan asked Cunningham to share her thoughts over the owner-fan interaction, which is when she addressed the overall fallout over her opinion that women's sports should be exclusive to biological women.

"I think I have a very clear and strong perspective on this," referring to the topic of trans athletes in women's sports. "I know that people are not always going to align and agree, I totally understand that, but I think the most important thing is having that respect, having that love, and pursuing peace in these conversations, in these debates, because I think that it's healthy.

"With that being said, I just hate how The W, the basketball of it all, is just getting overshadowed...It just makes me sad that all this sort of drama, on things that truly don't matter, that the basektball is getting overshadowed. "I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that,'" Cunningham told the outlet. "I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

"I'm very much in the middle. I agree with things on both sides, disagree with things on both sides," Cunningham continued." And that's all I've ever said about my political beliefs. But people love to assume."

item.title: One-wheeled AI security robot could patrol your property
item.description: The 1Rollo one-wheeled AI security robot uses a spinning flywheel to balance while patrolling properties at speeds up to 19 mph on a single charge.
item.content:encoded:
What if the next security guard rolling past your office had one wheel and never needed a coffee break? That is the pitch behind 1Rollo, a one-wheeled AI security robot from Estonian startup Rollo Robotics. The company believes its narrow design could patrol large properties at a lower operating cost than traditional security vehicles.

The machine follows mapped routes while watching the area around it. When its artificial intelligence detects unusual activity, 1Rollo can alert a human operator. That person can review the situation and decide whether to send a security guard.

For now, 1Rollo remains a functional prototype. Rollo Robotics says it plans to make the robot commercially available in 2027. Therefore, its design and specifications could change before customers begin using it.

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

HUMANOID ROBOT SKIN SENSES PEOPLE BEFORE CONTACT

1Rollo uses a 360-degree computer vision system to monitor its surroundings. It also relies on Real-Time Kinematic Global Navigation Satellite System positioning (RTK GNSS). RTK uses correction data to provide more precise positioning than standard satellite navigation. That precision could help the robot stay close to its assigned route around a business or industrial property. As the robot moves, its cameras and sensors look for obstacles. The system can then adjust its path to avoid a collision. Meanwhile, the AI analyzes the area for anomalies. If the system spots something unusual, it can send an alert over Wi-Fi or a 4G or 5G connection.

Keeping a 100-pound robot upright on one wheel takes more than a clever-looking design. Rollo Robotics uses a vertically positioned spinning flywheel inside the machine. The flywheel sits in line with the main wheel and helps the robot maintain its balance. To turn, the system tilts the internal flywheel toward either side. Rollo Robotics describes the hardware and software behind this method as patent-pending. The single-wheel design gives the robot a narrow footprint. As a result, it may travel through spaces where a wider patrol vehicle would struggle. However, Rollo Robotics has not published detailed performance results for stairs, steep slopes or deeply uneven ground. Those real-world tests will show where the monowheel design works best.

The company's current specifications list 1Rollo at about 43 inches tall. Its wheel measures 24 inches across, while the complete robot weighs approximately 100 pounds. Rollo Robotics lists a top speed of 19 mph. That is much faster than the walking pace of many existing security robots. Battery life reaches up to eight hours per charge, according to the company. The product information also lists autonomous wireless charging.

FOREIGN ROBOT BAN TARGETS CHINA OVER SECURITY FEARS

The standard robot includes a 360-degree vision system. However, Rollo Robotics designed the platform to support additional equipment. Customers could add thermal cameras for low-light environments. The platform can also support pan-tilt-zoom cameras for viewing activity farther away. Other compatible equipment includes night vision, RFID systems and custom payloads. These options could help companies adapt the robot for a specific property.

A cloud-based management platform would allow operators to monitor multiple robots from one location. Security teams could define patrol routes and review performance through the platform. An operator could also watch a live feed after receiving an alert. The robot includes a microphone and speaker. Therefore, the operator could speak with someone near the machine without immediately sending a guard. We have seen a similar approach with the Ascento Guard autonomous security robot. That machine also patrols property while human operators handle serious incidents.

However, robots still need to prove they provide meaningful results. Dublin, Ohio, recently retired an AI robot cop that recorded no arrests during its parking garage pilot. That case does not predict how 1Rollo will perform. Still, it shows why customers should establish clear goals before deploying autonomous security technology.

Rollo Robotics plans to offer 1Rollo through a Robotics-as-a-Service model. Customers would subscribe to the service instead of buying the robot outright. According to CEO and co-founder Sander Sebastian Agur, the subscription would include access to current hardware, software updates and support. The model could remove a large upfront equipment expense. It may also make repairs and future upgrades easier for customers. Rollo Robotics says its goal is to reduce operating costs compared with relying on human guards or patrol vehicles. However, the company has not announced subscription pricing.

A connected robot may improve physical security while creating new digital concerns. 1Rollo uses wireless connections and a cloud platform. Therefore, customers should ask how the company encrypts camera feeds and protects operator accounts. They should also ask where recordings are stored. Clear deletion policies will become important for employees and visitors who appear on camera. Meanwhile, the robot needs a safe way to handle a lost internet connection. It should keep avoiding people and obstacles even when a remote operator cannot reach it. Buyers should also learn how Rollo Robotics delivers security updates. A compromised patrol robot could expose video or provide unauthorized access to its controls. Lawmakers have already raised similar concerns about autonomous machines. A proposed federal bill would restrict government use of some foreign robots over national security fears. Rollo Robotics operates in Estonia, but every connected robot deserves the same cybersecurity review.

You probably will not find a one-wheeled robot guarding people's driveway anytime soon. However, businesses could begin seeing machines like 1Rollo around warehouses or office campuses. Large private properties may also use them to cover areas that guards cannot watch continuously. The robot could handle repetitive patrols while people make decisions during an incident. That may also keep guards away from hazardous areas until they understand what is happening. Still, a moving camera can feel more intrusive than one mounted on a wall. Employees and visitors deserve to know when the robot records them. They should also know who can watch the footage and how long the company keeps it. Those answers should arrive before the robot begins its first patrol.

1Rollo looks unusual, but the idea behind it makes sense. A narrow autonomous machine could cover large properties without the bulk of a security vehicle. The human operator also remains part of the process. The robot detects activity and sends an alert, while a person decides what should happen next. However, the polished demonstration is only the beginning. Rollo Robotics still needs to show that 1Rollo can handle changing weather, crowded spaces and long shifts without constant assistance. Pricing will play a major role too. Businesses need to know whether the subscription saves money and delivers better security than existing systems.

Would a one-wheeled AI guard make you feel safer, or would you wonder who was watching every time it rolled past? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: The 8 healthiest beans you should be eating more often, according to nutrition expert
item.description: A nutrition expert reveals the eight healthiest beans and legumes for protein, fiber and cholesterol benefits, plus easy ways to prep canned beans.
item.content:encoded:
Beans and legumes are affordable, protein-packed and health-promoting foods that deserve a more prominent place on your plate, health experts say.

"Fewer than 14% of American adults eat beans on a given day, and that's a problem, because they're some of the most nutrient-dense foods you can buy," New York City-based nutrition and wellness expert Samantha Cassetty, founder of Sam's Plate and co-author of "Sugar Shock," told Fox News Digital. "They deliver protein, fiber and slow-burning carbs for steady energy, plus folate, magnesium, iron and other essential nutrients."

Beans are also naturally cholesterol-free and contain no saturated fats, registered dietitian nutritionist Deborah Murphy told Food & Wine.

CHEAP, HEALTHY FOOD IS REJECTED BY MOST AMERICANS EVEN AS MAHA MOVEMENT PUSHES IT

Studies have linked regular bean consumption with a lower risk of chronic diseases, including heart disease, type 2 diabetes and obesity, which may contribute to a longer life expectancy.

"In a moment when everyone's chasing protein and grocery bills are climbing, canned beans are one of the cheapest proteins on the shelf," Cassetty said. "The best part is that you can open a can, rinse, drain and call it dinner prep."

Some beans and legumes stand out for their health benefits. 

Black beans are prized for their protein, fiber and antioxidants, Cassetty told Fox News Digital. They contain about 8 grams of protein and 8 grams of fiber per 1/2-cup serving.

One of Cassetty's go-to salads incorporates black beans, corn (frozen and canned work as well as fresh, she said), diced bell pepper, avocado, cherry tomatoes and a spoonful of salsa. She said it can be enjoyed as "a light meal, hearty side or wrap filling."

Technically a legume – the broader plant family beans belong to – chickpeas are versatile because they work in sweet and savory dishes alike, Cassetty said.

"Air-fry them for a crunchy snack or salad topper," she advised. 

"They're also great scattered over roasted veggies and grain bowls. Research shows people who eat chickpeas and hummus regularly have higher intakes of fiber, folate, potassium and iron than people who don't, and better overall diet quality scores."

Lentils are also legumes and offer a "ground-meat texture and a solid dose of plant-based iron," Cassetty said.

She recommended mixing them with chopped walnuts (Cassetty is a partner with the California Walnut Board) for extra fiber, protein and plant-based omega-3s.

"That combo of beans and walnuts is powerful, supporting heart, brain and gut health in each bite. Use the crumble in spaghetti sauce, tacos or wraps."

Edamame are immature soybeans that people typically boil or steam and eat as a snack or appetizer with coarse salt. They're also used in many dishes.

"Frozen edamame is a freezer staple in my house," Cassetty said. "A 1/2 cup delivers about 9 grams of protein and 4 grams of fiber. Toss it with cucumber, brown rice, rice vinegar, tamari and sesame oil for a five-minute meal."

White beans also pack a powerful protein punch, with about 9 grams of the essential nutrient per 1/2 cup.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"I stir them into tuna and egg salad, but my favorite trick is blending leftovers into a smoothie," Cassetty said. "You won't notice next to the sweetness of the fruit, but they add the creamiest texture, plus protein and fiber."

Pinto beans may have "a special edge on cholesterol," Cassetty said.

While the soluble fiber in all beans helps clear cholesterol from the bloodstream, animal research suggests they may lower cholesterol synthesis in the liver and cholesterol absorption in the small intestine, Cassetty said.

"In one trial, a half cup of pinto beans a day dropped total and LDL cholesterol by more than 8%, outperforming oatmeal," she said.

If you're planning to eat a high-fat meal – think a bacon cheeseburger with onion rings – you may want to find a way to incorporate kidney beans in the mix.

Animal research suggests kidney beans can favorably shift gut bacteria and reduce inflammatory markers associated with a high-fat diet, Cassetty noted. She advised using them in chili or over nachos, or trying them in a three-bean salad with some roughly chopped toasted walnuts for crunch and added nutritional value.

The protein, fiber and iron in black-eyed peas mean they deserve "a permanent spot in your bean rotation," Cassetty said.

They're also "the unsung hero of cowboy caviar," a cold bean salad that also uses fresh vegetables, herbs and vinaigrette dressing and is typically served with tortilla chips, she said.

item.title: Thomas Rhett reveals why he and wife Lauren reject celebrity perks for country life
item.description: The country singer says wife, Lauren Akins, craves simplicity and normalcy, admitting the rush of performing for thousands made him struggle at home.
item.content:encoded:
Thomas Rhett admitted this week that his wife didn’t think he was going to become a famous country singer.

"We've definitely had our fair share of ups and downs, ‘cause I think that Lauren really… she craves simplicity, at all costs, simplicity," the country singer said on the "Girls In Low Places" podcast on Sunday, clarifying that she believed he was talented, but knew that stardom was rare.

"She grew up, you know, real country, and her and her daddy would lay in the street at night and look at the stars," noting that "he would just call out different constellations and stuff like, ‘That's a satellite and that's this.’" 

He explained that was how she saw her life, calling it "a real suburban neighborhood thing."

Rhett said he and Lauren Akins have known each other since they were in first grade, and they briefly dated in high school before reconnecting after she graduated from college.

MARCUS MUMFORD SAYS BIBLE CAMP SPARKED DECADES-LONG LOVE STORY WITH WIFE CAREY MULLIGAN

"So, we got married at 22."

Admitting "there’s nothing normal" about fame, they noted that it affects everyone.

"There's just so many crazy things that come with being famous," he said, giving the example of getting to cut lines, which he said he refuses to do.

"I think that's why so many people try to just live their life in search of such normalcy and I think my wife obviously has wanted that her whole life, and we do live very simply," the "Die a Happy Man" singer said. "But it took me a minute."

He said his career "really started to pop" around 2017 to 2019.

"I don't think I let it get to my head, but I do think I got really used to it," the 36-year-old admitted. "In probably not the best way."
