Rhett admitted he has to actively focus on not letting fame get him, because "when you walk on stage in front of, you know, 10,000 people, that's like a rush that you can't like go replicate. You know what I'm saying? Like you can't just go like play flag football with your friends and think that's going to entice the same feeling."

For that reason, he has a difficult time "being content in simple situations because I think there's no super high going on."

That’s forced him to "get really good" at being quiet, which he says doesn't come naturally to him.

Hearing people singing his songs while he’s performing on stage has always seemed surreal, but the one that "gets" him is witnessing people cry when they meet him "because I don't see myself that way. Period."

"And I have, you know, definitely five kids that definitely don't see me that way," he joked.

The couple share Willa, 10, Ada, who turns 9 on Aug. 12, Lennon, 6, Lillie, 4, and Brave, who was born in February.

He admitted trying to be "super dad" and taking his kids to school while he’s in the middle of doing late-night concerts can also be exhausting.

Later, in the podcast, when asked what marriage advice he would give, Rhett said, "Don’t forget to continue to date your wife."

JESSIE JAMES DECKER ON WHY HER MARRIAGE TO ERIC DECKER HASN'T LOST ITS SPARK AFTER FOUR KIDS

"It gets so much harder when you have children to make time for each other because there's so many other bodies that need your full-time assistance," he explained.

The singer said he and his wife recently spent two days just the two of them in London before joining friends in the Cotswolds, noting that "you feel sad, and your kids are like ‘Why are you leaving?' And you're like, ‘Because we want to stay married!’" he joked.

Earlier this year, he admitted during his years of early fame he felt like he was "living a double life," adding that it almost ruined his marriage.

"I look through my life and I think about all the things that have kind of twisted me or made me like not the best person to be around, and it has always been either around affirmation or lack of affirmation," the country star told Sadie Robertson Huff on her "WHOA That’s Good" podcast.

GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'

Appearing on the podcast with his wife, Rhett said that at the height of his fame, he experienced "the most affirmation I think I'd ever received in my life. And I really liked it."

But he admitted that he didn’t feel he handled his marriage very well at the time.

"I look back at our life during that time, and I'm not — I don't think I stewarded it very well, to be honest with you," he said.

Rhett, who is Christian, said publicly he kept up a façade of spirituality, "but internally I was dying. Like I genuinely, I just liked what was happening so much that I think so much of me was being sucked into the world so hard that it just kept pushing me and her like this," he said, moving his hands away from each other.

Rhett noted that he and his wife said from "day one, divorce is not an option," but, "the more you actually think about it, anything is actually an option if you let it become that."

It wasn’t until 2020 that he "actually discovered bits and pieces of who I actually was at my core, without a microphone, without a stage with and without affirmation, because it was the first time it had ever been taken away from me, if that makes any sense," Rhett explained, referring to the pandemic.

"I’m not perfect," he continued. "I'll never be perfect, but I would say, like today, us looking at each other and being a married couple, I would say this is… I'm living my most true self now."

He pointed to his wife and added, "She always sort of has been."

item.title: Eyewitness describes suspicious encounter that helped launch Washington wildfire arson probe
item.description: A Washington grandfather says he spotted a stranger bent over near railroad tracks minutes before smoke erupted and the Old Trails Fire ignited.
item.content:encoded:
A Washington grandfather said a stranger lingering near a dead-end road where almost nobody goes immediately caught his attention – moments before smoke began rising from the same stretch of railroad tracks and a devastating wildfire erupted.

Paul Child was driving his grandson to pick up a friend Saturday when he noticed a bald man standing near the railroad tracks along West Euclid Road and staring into the tree line.

"I really didn’t think anything of it at that point," Child told Fox News Digital.

SPENCER PRATT REACTS TO SPOKANE DEVASTATION WITH BLUNT WILDFIRE WARNING AND MESSAGE OF FAITH

About 10 minutes later, Child drove back along the same road and noticed the man was still there.

"This time he was kind of bent over and looked like he was doing something in the brush or the bushes and the grass and the trees," Child said. "When he saw us, then he kind of stood up and was acting kind of nervous."

Even Child’s grandson sensed something was off.

"My grandson said, ‘What’s he doing?’" Child said.

The family returned to their home and minutes later, Child’s daughter, Ana Dillon, glanced toward the same stretch of railroad tracks.

"I just happened to look up and saw a huge cloud of white smoke, then black smoke," Dillon told Fox News Digital.

Child immediately connected the smoke to the stranger he had seen lingering near the tree line.

"The first thing I thought was, ‘That SOB started the fire,’" Child alleged.

MYSTERY STRANGER VANISHES AFTER FAMILY SAYS FRANTIC WARNING SAVED THEIR LIVES DURING DEVASTATING HOUSE FIRE

Child called 911 and tried to reach the only other homeowner on the dead-end stretch of road. The neighbor was not home, but Child reached him by phone and warned that a wildfire was moving toward the property, where workers were inside a shop behind the house.

"We drove down there and notified that person and told him maybe he should leave," Child said.

By then, firefighters had begun to arrive as flames spread across the dry grasslands and the family hurried to evacuate.

"The fire was coming toward us, so we packed up everything, everyone and animals," Dillon said.

PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT

Child said the family fled their nearly 17-acre property with five dogs and two cats, later flagging down an Airway Heights police officer and describing the man he had seen as a bald white male wearing a green T-shirt and backpack, court records show.

He also told officers where the man had been standing before smoke began rising from the area. Spokane County sheriff’s deputies soon detained a man matching the description.

Child, his grandson and the grandson’s friend then traveled with an Airway Heights police officer to where deputies were holding the suspect. Sitting inside Child’s pickup about 50 yards away, the three watched as deputies removed the man from a patrol vehicle and had him face them.

"The only thing I could really identify on him was his build and what he was wearing," Child said. "There was no question in any of our minds that was the individual we saw."

PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT DISPLAYED 'INCEL ENERGY,' MADE WOMAN UNCOMFORTABLE DURING UBER RIDE: PASSENGER

Authorities later arrested Aaron F. Farinacci on suspicion of first-degree arson, accusing him of intentionally setting the Old Trails Fire, the largest of three wildfires that destroyed hundreds of buildings and forced about 67,000 people to evacuate.

Child said the family did not learn until the following day that deputies had initially released Farinacci before arresting him after investigators developed additional evidence.

Court records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Farinacci was previously charged with first-degree murder after fatally shooting his father during an argument in Arizona in 2010. He later pleaded guilty to reduced charges of manslaughter and aggravated assault, served about eight years in prison and was released in 2020.

Learning about Farinacci’s criminal history turned the family’s initial relief into concern, Child said.

"He knew where I lived," Child said. "Then to come to find out what his history was, it’s kind of like ... this dude could have come back down here."

Child said the man initially caught his attention because strangers rarely venture onto the family’s road. The county permanently closed the dead-end stretch several years ago, leaving only two homes beyond the barricade.

"There hasn’t been a lot of trespassing now," Child said. "If we see somebody down there, a lot of times we take it upon ourselves to pull up and say, ‘Are you OK?’ ... Nine times out of 10, they’re gone after that."

Dillon said anyone lingering near the tracks would immediately stand out to the family.

"There’s only two houses on this street," she said. "If anyone is on this street, we most always call Crime Check. No one should be on this road. It’s a closed road. Anyone standing and kneeling down by the train tracks that’s not a city worker is a red flag."

While Child’s observations helped point investigators toward a suspect, retired Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives executive Scott Sweetow said eyewitness accounts are only the beginning of a wildfire arson investigation.

Fire investigators must first determine where a blaze started before they can establish how it ignited, Sweetow told Fox News Digital. That requires them to work backward from the aftermath, examine how the terrain and vegetation burned and eliminate plausible accidental causes.

"Arson fire in general is very hard to investigate," Sweetow said. "It requires a very meticulous focused effort that is not present in a lot of other investigations. And what complicates it is the fact that the evidence that you have to examine is often badly damaged by fire."

WHAT HAPPENED TO LEAVING THE GROOM AT THE ALTAR LIKE AN ADULT? BRIDE-TO-BE ACCUSED OF SETTING FIRE TO CHURCH

Investigators can reconstruct a fire’s earliest moments using witness accounts, video, cellphone data, first-responder observations and physical evidence. They also examine potential causes such as lightning, power infrastructure, trains, discarded smoking materials or other ignition sources.

That process can allow investigators to determine that a person started a fire even when no single item definitively establishes how it began, Sweetow said.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"It’s not magic. The grass doesn’t just burst into flame for no reason," Sweetow said. "So by eliminating all the causes that weren’t you figure out the cause that was, if that makes sense."

Sweetow cautioned against placing too much weight on any single piece of evidence, including investigators’ claim that Farinacci was carrying waterproof matches and a butane lighter when deputies first contacted him.

He said windproof and waterproof matches are more specialized than ordinary paper or wooden matches and are designed to remain lit in conditions that could extinguish a conventional match. Investigators would likely look for remnants of the same type of match near the fire’s point of origin, he said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"They’re very expensive. And they’re designed really almost like a little portable flare," Sweetow said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

The matches and lighter would still need to be considered alongside witness statements, physical evidence, electronic records and forensic findings. Sweetow said wildfire arson cases often depend on the combined weight of numerous facts rather than one decisive piece of evidence.

SEND US A TIP

He also said the decision to release Farinacci before arresting him after further investigation was not inherently unusual, particularly in a fast-moving emergency in which deputies were focused on evacuations and investigators had not yet completed their work.

GOT A TIP?

"I wouldn’t say it’s particularly unusual, it just seems like good police and investigator work to put the case together," Sweetow said.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Court records show fire investigators later concluded the blaze originated where Child reported seeing the man. They ruled out trains and nearby electrical infrastructure before determining the fire was consistent with dry grass being ignited by an open flame from a match or lighter.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

For Child, the investigation has been about the people whose homes and property were destroyed.

"My heart goes out to everybody," he said. "Hopefully the individual that caused all their pain and suffering is going to be held accountable for those actions."

item.title: Eric Adams battles tense crowd as Wisconsin audience erupts over AI data center proposal
item.description: Eric Adams was bombarded with boos and told he belongs "in prison" as he pitched a Wisconsin crowd on a controversial AI data center proposal.
item.content:encoded:
Former New York City Mayor Eric Adams struggled to get a word in as a Wisconsin audience bombarded him with boos and insults while he pitched the crowd on a proposed AI data center.

Adams was told he belongs "in prison" amid a barrage of fierce heckles during a wild eight-minute exchange that showed residents repeatedly interrupting the former mayor over his support for the proposed data center.

"You belong in prison!" one crowd member shouted, seemingly referencing Adams’ dismissed federal corruption case.

TEXAS GOV GREG ABBOTT EFFECTIVELY PAUSES NEW DATA CENTER PROJECTS PENDING STATEWIDE GRID AUDIT

Since leaving office, Adams has worked as a "pitchman" for several real estate-related technology companies, according to The Real Deal. He said he closes about 80% of the deals he pursues.

Adams appeared at the Wisconsin meeting on behalf of PNK Group, which is looking to develop a 209-acre data center at a former paper mill along the Wisconsin River.

"Whether we like it or not, folks, data centers are going to be here," Adams told the audience.

Many Wisconsin residents in the crowd opposed the proposal and let Adams know it throughout his presentation.

TOP ENERGY GROUP WARNS WEALTHY FOREIGNERS ARE POTENTIALLY BANKROLLING ANTI-DATA CENTER CAMPAIGNS ACROSS US

"You’re here to steal our water!" one resident shouted.

"Get out of here!" another resident shrieked.

"Put it in your backyard!" yet another said.

"Anyone can heckle, but not everybody can communicate," Adams said in response.

Adams offered to answer questions about the data center and engage in what he called a "dialogue."

The former NYC mayor urged the crowd to stop the "hate on technology," defending his stance with a personal anecdote, in which he said AI helped his doctor in his Type 2 diabetes diagnosis.

The audience, again, erupted in a loud chant of boos.

Adams attempted to regain the stage and tame the angry crowd. And although one audience member came to his defense, saying, "Let him talk!," he struggled to speak over the crowd of critics.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Adams’ chief communications officer Todd Shapiro said Hell Gate, which first reported the story, got the facts "wrong."

"A short video clip cannot accurately portray an event that lasted much longer," Shapiro wrote in part. "It omits the many attendees who approached Mayor Adams afterward to thank him, ask questions, and express appreciation for his willingness to engage directly with the community."

Shapiro also said Adams' support in proposing the Wisconsin data center is "helping communities better understand the economic opportunities that responsible AI and data center development can bring."

"Eric Adams has consistently supported policies that encourage responsible investment, create good-paying jobs, strengthen local tax bases, and position American communities to compete in the industries of the future," Shapiro told Fox News Digital.
